Q: Is there a std::map analogue of std::vector's emplace_back? A:

@PepijnKramer: "since maps are not ordered" - I'm not sure what you mean.
std::map is actually ordered.
The unordered version is std::unoredered_map.

Q: Concurrent cache using SoftReferences behaves unpredictably under memory pressure, how to fix? A:
  • Sometimes objects disappear from the cache unexpectedly, even when memory usage is low.

This is what the API docs say about when soft references are cleared:

All soft references to softly-reachable objects are guaranteed to have been cleared before the virtual machine throws an OutOfMemoryError. Otherwise no constraints are placed upon the time at which a soft reference will be cleared or the order in which a set of such references to different objects will be cleared. Virtual machine implementations are, however, encouraged to bias against clearing recently-created or recently-used soft references.

(Emphasis added.)

It is therefore unclear what basis you have for expectations about when soft references to softly reachable objects in your cache will be cleared. Certainly the docs do not require memory pressure for clearance of soft references to softly reachable objects, and neither does the Oracle / OpenJDK implementation.

  • Occasionally, cleanup() causes high CPU usage under heavy load.

It should not be surprising that iterating through a large map is expensive. Especially so a concurrent map with contended access, and even more so if many modifications are made along the way.

Iterating the whole map is not at all what you should be doing here. If you register your SoftReferences with a reference queue then you can discover exactly which ones to remove from the cache by obtaining them from that queue. And if you subclass SoftReference then you can endow yours with references to the corresponding cache keys, so that you know which entries to remove without searching at all.

You could optionally avoid having an explicit cleanup() method at all by establishing a thread devoted to retrieving references to the queue as they become available and removing them immediately.

  • I’m not sure this is thread-safe when cleanup() runs concurrently with get() and put().

ConcurrentHashMap is thread safe in the sense that no data races arise from multiple threads performing operations on the same instance concurrently. Individual actions by one thread have their documented behavior regardless of actions by other threads. However, sequences of actions on a ConcurrentHashMap by one thread can suffer from interference from intervening actions by other threads unless some additional mechanism is employed to prevent it. This is not different from a Hashtable or a synchronized Map provided by Collections.synchronizedMap(). In your case, nothing in the specs for ConcurrentHashMap guarantees that the state of the map observed by your entry.getValue().get() is the same state affected by the subsequent it.remove(). Suppose, then, that a thread retrieves a SoftReference from the cache, observes it to have been cleared, and therefore constructs and caches a new a new one. It is possible that in the meantime, a thread running cleanup() also notices the cleared reference and therefore moves to drop it from the cache, but instead ends up removing the newly cached one. A similar sequence of events could result in distinct objects for the same key being live at the same time.

These are not necessarily failure cases for you per se, so maybe you don't want to account them thread safety issues, but they could certainly make your cache less effective.

  • Are there any concurrency issues with this implementation, especially with hundreds of threads?

See above. But also, hundreds of concurrently running platform threads could be its own concurrency issue. Context switching is expensive.

  • How do SoftReferences interact with GC under different memory pressures? Why might cached objects disappear unexpectedly?

Under sufficient memory pressure, SoftReferences to softly-reachable objects may be cleared sooner than they otherwise would be. Lack of memory pressure is not a good reason to think that soft references will go uncleared indefinitely.

Q: Close and restart shell after running 'conda init' A:

For some additional context, what it is telling you is that the shell's initialization files have been updated. But the current shell was initialized before those changes were made, so the easiest way to reload everything reliably is to type exit and start a new shell. Whatever you did to start the current shell (probably running in a terminal window, or on a text console if you're really old school), do it again.

There is no compelling need to stop the current shell instance; just understand that it does not contain the modifications which Conda made to its initialization files. You could simply leave it open and open a second terminal where a new shell will be loaded with the up-to-date configuration. (But obviously, remember that the old shell running in the first terminal window does not have the full capabilities to support Conda that the new one does.)

You could stop reading here.

If you know what you are doing, you can selectively load the changed files, or examine what was added, and run it at the command line in the old shell.

The simple and brutal solution in your example is to type source /root/.bashrc at the Bash prompt in the terminal where you received this message. But understand that this could duplicate some previous actions which were taken the first time the .bashrc was sourced, when your current shell instance was started. You should examine your Bash startup files and understand what's in them before you blindly plunge ahead ... or be prepared to notice that it didn't work like you hoped, and fall back to exiting the current shell and starting a new one.

In some more detail, a properly written .bashrc should be idempotent, i.e. make sure that it can be run a second or third etc time without adverse side effects. Typically this happens by examining whether a change to the environment is necessary before making it. So, for example, a crude hack would be to just add $HOME/bin to the beginning of the PATH unconditionally, which means that if you source .bashrc again, you end up with the same directory in your PATH twice (not generally a significant problem, but there could be consequences if you have stuff in your private PATH which should not override some other tool's preferred implementation)

PATH=$HOME/bin:$PATH

... whereas if done completely properly, your Bash startup files would only add the directory to your PATH if it's not there already:

case :$PATH: in
  *:$HOME/bin:*) ;;          # it's already there; do nothing
  *) PATH=$HOME/bin:$PATH ;; # it's not there; add it
esac

Your shell's startup file could contain basically anything. If starting a new shell has the side effect of launching a manned mission to Mars, you will now have two of them. But this brief exposition ends here.

If you know what was in your .bashrc before, you can see what was added, and just run that. Maybe you see something like

bash$ diff /root/.bashrc~ /root/.bashrc  # lucky I made a backup in /root/.bashrc~
2022a2023,2025
> 
> # Stuff added by Conda
> eval $(/opt/random/path/to/conda.init.bash)

(I don't know what Conda adds; this is just a speculative example.)

Here, you can see that eval $(/opt/random/path/to/conda.init.bash) was the thing which was added since the previous time you edited your .bashrc, so that's the thing you want to run in your current shell as well in order to bring it up to date.

Generally, you can expect the changes to be added to the end of the file, though there is no guarantee that some tools might not make more sophisticated changes.

If other files were changed, you have to understand what they are for, and manually execute the same changes in the current shell.

Q: How to convert Julian date to calendar date on Hive? A:

Julian Date Format -- yyyyDDD The Date Format which is expected -- 'yyyy-MM-dd'

from_unixtime(unix_timestamp(cast(**julianl_date_col** as string),'yyyyDDD'),'yyyy-MM-dd')

Q: Is it possible to use the values method for a HashMap if the values are ArrayLists? A:

Your Map#values call returns
Collection < ArrayList < Object > >

The Answer by maress is correct. No need for arrays. Just loop the collection returned by Map#values. In your case, each element in the Collection is an ArrayList < Object > according to your prose.

That Answer correctly shows you how to use the enhanced for loop to examine each of the list values.

Streams

Alternatively, in modern Java we could use streams instead of that for loop.

HashMap < Integer, ArrayList < Object > > map = … ;
Object target = … ;
boolean contains = 
    map
        .values()     // Returns `Collection < ArrayList < Object > >` according to your Question. 
        .stream()     // Make a stream where each element is a list of objects. 
        .filter( list -> list.contains( target ) ) 
        .findAny()    // Returns an `Optional`. Stops filtering upon the first hit. 
        .isPresent()  // The `Optional` is empty if no list was found to contain your target. 
;

I don’t know that a stream is better than a for loop in this particular situation. But it is an option.
